corrected_value.title: Bias at the Beeb: A quantitative study of slant in BBC online reporting

decisions.quote:
A fortnight ago, the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS) published the report
                              ‘Bias at the Beeb: A quantitative study of slant in BBC online reporting’,
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 2593 and blind target 0 identify the same tested original study: the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS) report 'Bias at the Beeb: A quantitative study of slant in BBC online reporting'. In the primary text, there is no reference list, no individual author name printed (the text refers only to 'the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS)' and 'its author', never printing 'Latham'), no DOI, and no explicit citation year printed alongside the title (moreover, the blog post is dated September 2nd, 2013, states the report was published 'A fortnight ago', and notes its analysis period ended 31st May 2013, contradicting shipped's year '2012'). Blind coding accurately records the verbatim title printed in the text and leaves unprinted citation metadata blank per the codebook.

decisions.quote:
In order to dig deeper into the results obtained by the CPS, I have tried to replicate this part of the
   research. Of course, without access to the CPS dataset there will be some differences from their
   results, but the methodology I have applied is designed to be transparent and robust in its own
   right.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind correctly classify the record as a replication. Without access to the original CPS dataset, the author independently collected and coded a fresh dataset of 364 BBC Online news stories from 01/06/2010 to 31/05/2013 to re-test the CPS report's findings.

decisions.quote:
These numbers are all indicative, prior to any reliability testing, and, of course, they do not
   realistically provide evidence of the existence or absence of bias in the BBC any more than the
   CPS figures do. What they do represent is a fairly simple way to debunk the main conclusions
   drawn by the CPS from their own analysis and then spread by an overly­credulous press.
decisions.reason: In replicating the second part of the CPS report (coding BBC Online stories mentioning the ten think tanks for 'health warnings' and descriptions as 'independent'), the author obtained empirical proportions that mirrored the CPS findings ('the "health warning" proportions I found are relatively similar to those of the CPS'; 'This backs up the CPS conclusion that health warnings are more likely to be applied to right-wing think tanks, which are also less likely to be described as "independent"'; 'While the contextualisation data ("health warnings" and descriptions of independence) certainly mirror the CPS findings...'). However, the central thesis of the replication is that the CPS methodology and its omission of total mention counts (where right-wing think tanks actually accounted for 55% of mentions versus 45% for left/centre) mean those figures do not validly demonstrate ideological bias at the BBC, thereby debunking the main conclusions drawn by the CPS. Under the codebook, obtaining the original empirical effect while arguing as the main message that the original method/analysis does not validly support the substantive claim is coded as 'statistically successful but flawed' rather than 'failed'.
